title: Accounting of the soul
hookLine: a daily honest review of one's actions

lines: THE SHOP CLOSES FOR THE NIGHT.
cards: A shop owner closes up for the night. The door is locked, the sign is flipped, and before going home she sits down with the register and the receipts. What came in.
What went out. Where the numbers don't match. It's ten quiet minutes, and it's the reason the shop is still open next year.
Jewish teachers of character took that end-of-day ledger and turned it inward: the same honest columns, but the business is your own day.

teach.b: Cheshbon hanefesh. Cheshbon is an accounting, a reckoning, the word on a bill. Hanefesh means of the soul.
Four turns. First, a verse in Lamentations: "Let us search and try our ways, and return to the LORD." Search and try, not glance: a real look, the way you'd go through a drawer, not just open it.
In the book of Numbers there's an old song that begins, come to Heshbon, the name of a city.

The Talmud, in tractate Bava Batra, hears the name as cheshbon and reads the line as advice: come, let us make an accounting of the world, what a good deed costs against what it gains, what a wrong gains against what it costs.
A place on a map becomes a habit of the heart. Third, daily, not yearly. The season before Yom Kippur is known for a great yearly accounting.
Mussar teachers asked for something smaller and more often: a short review each day, often at night, before sleep. Small enough that a single sharp word doesn't get lost in a year of them.
Fourth, honest, not harsh. A good bookkeeper doesn't scream at the receipts; she writes down what's there. No beating yourself up, no polishing the story.
What happened. What it cost someone. What you'd do with the moment back.
And it counts the income too: the kind word, the patience you managed, the trait you measured right.

how: Jews traditionally make a cheshbon hanefesh in the season before Yom Kippur, and in Mussar practice it is often done briefly each night: a calm review of the day's actions, sometimes written in a notebook, focused on one trait.

o: a list of sins confessed aloud in synagogue
a yearly tally of money owed to charity
an honest nightly review of your own actions

p: read as: come, let us account

s: an accounting of the soul only happens before Yom Kippur
Mussar teachers asked for a short review each day, often at night.
the Talmud reads a city's name as a call to take account
in Bava Batra, come to Heshbon becomes come, let us make an accounting.
the point of the review is to punish yourself
honest, not harsh: write down what's there, and count the good too.

games.q: it's night, and in your review you find a sharp word you said at lunch. what does the practice ask?
o: skip it; the day is over.
look at it plainly: what happened, what it cost, what you'd do with it back.
replay it for an hour and feel terrible.
games.why: a cheshbon hanefesh is a bookkeeper's look: honest, not harsh, and small enough to do every night.

practice: Walk through your day from this morning to now, like scrolling back through photos.

Stop at one moment that went well and let it count, then at one you'd like back, and look at it plainly, what happened and what it cost someone, with no sentencing and no excuses; if it helps, look only for the trait you've been measuring.
If you pray, bring the ledger to God in your own words; if not, close the book gently.

wordCard.voice: Cheshbon hanefesh. An accounting of the soul: an honest review of your own actions, done in Mussar practice day by day, often before sleep. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: an accounting of the soul.

carryVoice: Your line: account for the soul. The ledger counts the income too, not just the losses. Rest well tonight.
